name: David Evans

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, David. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, so feel free to say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for a repairs and refurbishment contractor that does all the council and housing association homes on the Westgate estates. Most days it's carpentry on old flats, new fire doors, rotten window frames out, kitchens in, and lately a lot of insulation work behind new stud walls. I start with my phone, the job list comes through on an app and I measure rooms with the camera, which saves me an hour a day. What I love is that the tenants are mostly older folk who are really glad to see you. What wears me out is the damp and the fact that the jobs are booked too tight.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: You mentioned the phone saves you an hour. How much do you use these tools?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Every day, honestly. I talk my job notes into the phone and an AI tidies them into a report, and I use it to translate with Andrei, who's from Romania and still learning English. My partner Meera thinks I'm a bit of a gadget fiend. I tried running my own firm six years ago and it went under, so we're still paying off that loan, and we've got maybe a fortnight of money spare. There's this contractor and not much else round here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm a bit disappointed, to be honest. I'd tell the lads it was always going to be handy tools rather than magic. Online I'd probably post something about how the useful bits are the boring ones, like reports and measuring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's fine. I keep the tools I've already got, the job doesn't change, and I keep paying off the loan. I'd still be on lower pay than I should be, but AI was never going to fix that, the contract rates are the problem.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the measuring and report apps and try a couple of new ones as they come out. I'd keep pushing the union to get our contractor to pay for proper kit, like decent tablets, instead of us using our own phones. And I'd keep chipping away at the loan, about two hundred a month, which has another two years to run.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, with a little bit of 'is that it?'.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use your own phone for work. How do you feel about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It annoys me, because the company gets all the benefit and I pay for the data. Last winter my screen cracked on a scaffold and I paid ninety to fix it. I raised it at the branch meeting and three others said the same. It's small, but small things add up when you've got nothing spare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said AI was never going to fix the pay. What would?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A better contract between the council and the firm, honestly. The council picks the cheapest bid, the firm squeezes us, and the tenants get rushed jobs. If the council paid a fair rate and wrote fair pay into the contract, that'd do more than any app.

S0.say: I'm a bit disappointed, since it was always going to be handy tools rather than magic. The useful bits are the boring ones, like reports and measuring.
S0.think: It's fine for me, I keep my tools and the job stays the same. Pay stays low, but that's down to contract rates, not AI.
S0.do: Keeps using measuring and report apps and tries new ones as they appear. Pushes the union to get the contractor to pay for work tablets, and keeps paying about two hundred a month on the loan from his failed firm.
S0.feel: Calm, with a bit of 'is that it?'.
S0.quote: Last winter my screen cracked on a scaffold and I paid ninety to fix it.
S0.fieldNote: David is the rare older tradesman who is mildly disappointed that AI didn't do more. He sees low pay as a political problem in council contracts, not a technology problem. The failed business left debt but also left him unafraid of risk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment for unions and councils to get ahead of it, with training paid for by the firms that save money. At work I'd tell the older lads it's not as scary as it looks, I'd show them on my phone. Online I'd be one of the people saying, look, here's how to use it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd do all right in this one. Retrofit, the insulation and energy work, is growing, and the people who can use the scanning and planning tools will be the ones they keep. My worry is more for Andrei and the older lads who won't touch it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up this winter for the retrofit assessor course at the college, the one where you survey homes and plan the insulation, it's about four hundred and the union pays half. I'd learn every new tool the firm brings in and offer to train others. And I'd push the branch to get a written deal that nobody over 55 gets let go without a training offer first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit excited even. I'd have a job I'm good at that isn't just my knees.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said four hundred for the course with half paid. Can you afford two hundred right now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Barely. It'd mean skipping a loan payment and ringing the bank to explain, which I hate. Meera would say do it, because she watched me come back from the firm going bust and she knows I need something to aim at. We'd eat a lot of soup that month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the older lads who won't touch it. Who are you thinking of?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's Phil, 61, best joiner I've ever worked with, and he won't even use the job app, he rings the office. In this picture he's the first one they push out, and that's wrong. I'd sit with him in the van at lunch and show him, slowly, without anyone watching.

S1.say: This is the moment for unions and councils to get ahead of it, with training paid for by the firms that save money. I'd show people on my phone how to use the tools.
S1.think: I'd do all right, because retrofit work is growing and people who can use scanning and planning tools will be kept. My worry is for Andrei and the older lads who won't touch it.
S1.do: Signs up this winter for a retrofit assessor course costing about four hundred, half paid by the union. Learns every new tool, offers to train colleagues like Phil, and pushes the branch for a deal that nobody over 55 is let go without a training offer.
S1.feel: Calm and a little excited about a job that isn't only about his knees.
S1.quote: There's Phil, 61, best joiner I've ever worked with, and he won't even use the job app, he rings the office.
S1.fieldNote: This is the picture David almost wants: change he can ride with skills he already has. His progressive streak shows in wanting firms to pay for training and protecting older colleagues. Thin money still bites, since even half a course fee means a missed loan payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly what happens when nobody regulates, and the government needs to step in now, with income support and a slower rollout. At work I'd stop being the cheerful gadget guy for a while. Online I'd be arguing for a basic income and public ownership of the robots, or at least a share of what they earn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, even I'd be scared. I can learn tools, but if the tool does the whole job, being good with it only buys you a few months. At 60 with a loan and two weeks of money, that's a real problem.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the two years before, I'd try to get onto whatever robot crews the firm trials, as the person who sets them up and checks their work, because someone has to sign it off. I'd cut everything, Meera and I would drop the car to one and stop the bits of help we give our daughter. I'd join every campaign the union runs for income support, and I'd write to our member of parliament, which I've never done.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that, with only two years' warning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. My adaptability usually calms me down, but this is too fast for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said someone has to sign off the robots' work. Do you think that job would last?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For a while. Tenants will want a person to blame when the robot fits a door upside down, and the council will want a name on the safety form. But how many of those jobs? Maybe one person for every five of us now. I'd want to be that one, and I feel guilty saying it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why guilty?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because if I get the one job, Phil and Andrei don't. I believe in all of us coming through together, it's what I vote for. But when there's a loan letter on the mat, you look after your own house first. I don't like that about myself.

S2.say: This is what happens without regulation, and the government must step in now with income support and a slower rollout. I'd argue for a basic income and a public share in what the robots earn.
S2.think: Even I'd be scared, because if the tool does the whole job, being good with it only buys a few months. At 60 with a loan and two weeks of money, that's a real problem.
S2.do: Tries in the two years before to get onto the firm's robot trials as the person who sets up and signs off their work. Cuts to one car and stops helping their daughter, and joins union campaigns and writes to his member of parliament for the first time.
S2.feel: Alarmed, because this is too fast for his usual adaptability to calm him.
S2.quote: I can learn tools, but if the tool does the whole job, being good with it only buys you a few months.
S2.fieldNote: Even the most adaptable of the trade finds the fast picture beyond him, and he says so. He openly names the clash between his values and his instinct to grab the one remaining job. He blames lack of regulation and turns to politics as well as his own moves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to do this right if we start today, so no excuses. At work I'd be back to showing people how to use things. Online I'd push for a training fund for older trades workers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gets me to 63, and by then I'd have the assessor course done and maybe some robot setup experience. I think I'd land somewhere, maybe not well paid, but somewhere. And the loan would be gone by then, which matters a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the assessor course in the first year and ask to be on any robot trial from day one. I'd clear the loan, two years left, and then put that two hundred a month into savings instead. I'd start a little evening thing showing older tradespeople how to use the apps, maybe at the union hall, because that's where I'm useful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does that feel compared with the two-year picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but I'd feel like I was driving, not being driven.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said not well paid but somewhere. What's the lowest you'd accept?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take less than I earn now if it was steady and indoors, I'm not proud. If a supervisor job paid what I get now, I'd bite their hand off. The thing I can't do is nothing, I tried that for three months after the firm went bust and I nearly went mad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happened in those three months?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I sat at home, sent out applications, and watched daytime TV. Meera came home and found me asleep at four in the afternoon one day and she just looked at me. Next morning I took a labouring job at half my rate. So whatever this picture brings, I'd be moving.

S3.say: Five years is enough to do this right if we start today, so there are no excuses. I'd push for a training fund for older trades workers.
S3.think: By 63 I'd have the assessor course and maybe robot setup experience, so I'd land somewhere, maybe not well paid. The loan would be gone by then too.
S3.do: Does the assessor course in the first year and joins robot trials from day one. Clears the loan and saves the two hundred a month afterwards, and runs evening sessions at the union hall teaching older tradespeople to use the apps.
S3.feel: Uneasy, but feeling like he's driving rather than being driven.
S3.quote: Meera came home and found me asleep at four in the afternoon one day and she just looked at me.
S3.fieldNote: Five years is enough for David to set himself up, and the loan ending matters as much as the training. His story of three idle months after his business failed explains why doing nothing scares him more than lower pay. He'd turn his skill with tools into helping others.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years means nobody has an excuse, councils, firms, government, all of them. I'd tell the apprentices to learn both, the hands and the screen. Online I'd keep sharing what's working and what isn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2036 I'm 68, so I'd be at the end anyway. With ten years I could do the course, work my way into a setup or inspection role, and finish on my own terms. The kids' generation is the real question, not me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With a decade's warning, what would you actually do, now and in the first year after it arrives?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working on the estates, do the assessor course in the next couple of years, and slowly move into inspecting and signing off work. I'd clear the loan and save after that. I'd vote and campaign for public retraining money, because I want Andrei and the young ones to get what I'd get.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, really. Ten years is a long time in my life, I've changed jobs in less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you've changed jobs in less than ten years. What do you mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the last ten years I've been employed, self-employed, bust, labouring, and back to this. So ten years of warning feels like forever. I know that sounds strange from a man with two weeks of savings, but that's how I feel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You keep mentioning Andrei. What would happen to him in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He's 34, so he'd be 44 when it lands, with two little ones. He's sharp, he'd learn anything, but his English holds him back on paperwork. If I could help him with the language and the tools over ten years, he'd be fine. That's one thing I'd do.

S4.say: Ten years means councils, firms and government have no excuse. I'd tell apprentices to learn both the hands and the screen.
S4.think: I'd be 68 and at the end anyway, so I could retrain and finish on my own terms. The younger generation is the real question, not me.
S4.do: Keeps working on the estates, does the assessor course in the next couple of years and moves into inspecting and signing off work. Clears the loan and saves afterwards, campaigns for public retraining money, and helps his colleague Andrei with language and tools.
S4.feel: Calm, because ten years feels long to someone who has changed jobs in less.
S4.quote: So ten years of warning feels like forever.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade David is calm despite thin savings, because he trusts his ability to change and will be near the end of his working life. His main concern moves to younger colleagues like Andrei. He links his own plans to a wider political demand for public retraining money.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one. Two years is less time than it took me to get over the firm going bust. What would help is a basic income or some wage support while people switch, and a rule that firms using robots on council contracts have to keep a share of the old workforce and train them. The public pays for those contracts, so the public should get a say.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask people what they lost last time. I lost my business, and nobody asked me what would have helped then either. If you only ask about the future, you miss that most of us are still paying for the past.

headlineQuote: If you only ask about the future, you miss that most of us are still paying for the past.
portrait: David Evans is a 58-year-old repairs carpenter on council and housing association estates, a self-confessed gadget fiend who uses AI every day for measuring, reports and translating for his colleague Andrei. A failed business six years ago left him with a loan, two weeks of savings and no fear of change. He's calm in the Plateau and almost keen in Steady Disruption, where he plans a retrofit assessor course. AGI by 2028 alarms him even so, and he admits he'd chase the last job signing off robot work despite his beliefs. With five or ten years he feels in control again and turns his attention to helping others through.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because two years is less time than it took him to recover from his firm going bust.
whatWouldHelp: Wage support or a basic income during the switch, and rules making firms on council contracts keep and train a share of the old workforce.
